blocks.prompt: The Tree That Keeps Its Leaves All Winter
blocks.text: Most trees drop all their leaves when fall comes. By winter their branches are bare. The pine tree does not do that. Its leaves are needles. A needle is skinny and tough, with a waxy coat that holds water in. Cold wind cannot dry it out. So the pine tree keeps its needles all winter long. It stays green while the other trees stand bare. The pine tree is shaped like a triangle. Snow lands on the branches and slides right off. Up in the branches, the tree makes cones. Seeds hide inside the cones, waiting for spring.

blocks.prompt: Why the Pine Stays Green
blocks.text: In the fall, an oak or a maple pulls the good stuff out of its leaves, drops them, and waits out the winter bare. That works, but it costs the tree a whole season. The pine tree made a different deal. A pine leaf is a needle: thin, stiff, and wrapped in a layer of wax. Water escapes from a wide flat leaf quickly. A needle has almost no surface for water to escape from, and the wax seals in the rest. Freezing wind cannot dry it out, so the pine keeps its needles through the snow. Each needle stays on the branch for two years or more, and the tree drops them a few at a time instead of all at once. That is why a pine can work on a warm winter afternoon while the maple next to it is still asleep. Up in the branches sit the cones. A pine cone is a case full of seeds. When the weather turns dry, the scales open and the seeds spin away on papery wings.

blocks.prompt: The Needle and the Cone
blocks.text: Every leaf has the same problem: it must open itself to the air to feed the tree, and every moment it stays open it loses water. A broadleaf tree like a maple solves this by giving up. In autumn it drains its leaves of anything valuable, cuts them loose, and spends the winter shut down. A pine refuses to shut down. Its answer is the needle. Roll a leaf up until it is almost a wire, coat it in wax, and sink its breathing pores into little grooves below the surface, and you have built a leaf that barely leaks. Frozen ground cannot hand up much water, so a pine's greatest winter danger is not cold but drought. The needle is a drought-proof leaf. It stays on the branch for two years, sometimes far longer, and the tree replaces its needles gradually rather than all at once. So on any mild day, in any month, a pine is quietly making food while the bare trees around it wait. The cone is the other half of the design. Pines do not make flowers or fruit. Small soft cones release clouds of yellow pollen into the spring wind, and the wind, not a bee, carries it to the woody cones on the same tree or the next one. Then the pine takes its time. In most pines nearly two years pass between pollination and a ripe seed. When the seeds are finally ready, the cone waits for dry weather, because damp air would drop the seeds straight down. On a dry day the scales curl open and each seed sails out on a thin papery wing, spinning as it goes.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Genus Pinus: about 120 species
Needles: low surface area, waxy cuticle, sunken stomata
Winter is a drought problem, not only a cold one
Resin seals wounds and traps insects
Amber is fossilized conifer resin
Cone scales open in dry air and close in damp

blocks.prompt: Built for Bad Weather
blocks.text: Consider the trade a tree makes with the weather. Leaves are food factories, and a factory only pays if it runs. A maple builds cheap, wide, thin leaves, runs them hard through a warm summer, then throws the whole set away in autumn and stands empty for six months. That works beautifully where summers are long. Move north, or up a mountain, or onto thin sandy soil, and the math stops working. There is not enough summer to pay for a new set of leaves every year. This is the country the pines took. A pine needle is a leaf engineered for hardship. It is rolled into a narrow cylinder, which gives it very little surface for its volume, and surface is where water is lost. It is sealed under a thick waxy cuticle. Its stomata, the pores it breathes through, sit sunk in rows below the surface, sheltered from moving air. The result is a leaf so miserly with water that it can stay open for business in weather that would shrivel a maple leaf in an afternoon. That matters more than it sounds, because winter is not really a cold problem for a tree. It is a drought problem. When the ground is frozen, the roots can pull up almost nothing, so any leaf that leaks is a leak the tree cannot repay. The pine's needles leak so little that they can hang on for two years or more, and the tree sheds them a few at a time rather than all at once. It never stands empty. On a mild day in February, when the maples are still bare sticks, a pine is already working. The rest of the tree keeps the same argument. The narrow triangle shape lets snow slide off branches that would otherwise snap under the load. Springy branches bend instead of breaking. Thick resin floods any wound, seals it against rot, and glues up insects that try to bore in. That resin, hardened and buried for millions of years, is what we call amber. None of this is free. A needle is expensive to build, and a pine grows more slowly than a maple in a good year. But pines are not competing for good years. They are holding the ground where the weather is hard, and there they win. Pines cover cold northern forests, dry mountain slopes, and poor sandy soils across the northern half of the world, in about 120 different species.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Pinus mundayi: oldest known pine fossil, about 140 million years
Sealed cones need roughly 122F of heat to open
Bristlecone needles can work for 30 to 40 years
Methuselah, a bristlecone, is about 4,850 years old
Fertilization comes about a year after pollination
Cone scales move by swelling, no living cells needed

blocks.prompt: The Tree That Learned to Wait
blocks.text: A pine tree looks like a simple thing standing in the cold. It is actually an argument about time, and the pine has been making that argument for a very long while. Start with the leaf. A maple leaf is a bet on a good summer: build it wide and cheap, run it hard for five months, discard it, repeat. Where summers are long and soil is rich, that bet pays. Where they are not, it bankrupts the tree. A pine needle is the opposite bet. It is rolled into a narrow cylinder, so it carries almost no surface for its volume, and surface is where water escapes. It is sealed under a heavy waxy cuticle. Its stomata, the pores through which it breathes, are sunk in grooves below the surface, out of the wind. A needle is slow and expensive to build, but it lasts. Most pine needles work for two to five years. On a Great Basin bristlecone pine, high in the White Mountains of California, a single needle may still be working thirty or forty years after it opened. That patience is the whole strategy, because winter does not kill trees with cold so much as with thirst. Frozen ground gives the roots nothing to pull up, and a leaky leaf in February is a debt the tree cannot pay. The pine's needles leak so little that it can keep every one of them, shedding a few at a time instead of stripping bare. So the pine is never shut down. Give it one mild afternoon in midwinter and it is making food while the hardwoods around it are still empty sticks. Now consider fire, which the pine did not merely survive but learned to use. The oldest pine we have found, Pinus mundayi, comes from Nova Scotia and is about 140 million years old. We know it exists because it burned: the fossil is charcoal. Pines and fire have been in the same room from the beginning. Some pines answer fire with armor. A mature ponderosa grows bark in thick plates and drops its lower branches, so a ground fire runs past its ankles and leaves the crown untouched. Other pines answer with timing. The cones of the lodgepole and the jack pine are sealed shut with hard resin, and they can hang closed on the branch for years. Only heat around 122 degrees Fahrenheit melts that seal. A fire sweeps through, the forest burns, and in the quiet afterward the cones creak open and drop their seeds onto warm ash with no shade and no competition anywhere. The tree does not fear the fire. It waits for it. Even the ordinary cone is a machine for reading weather. Pines make no flowers and no fruit. Soft pollen cones puff yellow clouds into the spring wind, and the wind carries the pollen to the woody seed cones, where fertilization may not happen for a year. Roughly two years pass between pollination and a ripe seed. When the seeds are ready, the cone still will not release them in damp air, because a seed dropped in the wet falls straight down. The scales are built from two layers that swell at different rates, so the cone opens in dry weather and closes when it rains, with no cells, no signal, and no life required. A cone on a shelf in your house will still do it. Then there is the resin. Any wound floods with it, and it hardens into a plug that seals out rot and traps the insects that try to bore in. Bury that resin for fifty million years and it becomes amber. Slow leaf, patient cone, armored bark, sealed wound. None of it is fast. All of it is durable. The bristlecone that assembled itself out of these parts on a dry mountain has now been standing for about 4,850 years, which means it was already a mature tree when the first pyramid was built.
